svg.title: Hardening priorities P0, P1 and P2: what to do first, what it stops, and what to refuse to do at all
svg.desc: Three columns of priority. P0, do it this week, eight items: no management address reachable from the internet, SSH only with telnet and HTTP disabled, unique local credentials plus TACACS, SNMPv3 or nothing, out-of-band or management VRF, NTP working, config backup automated and off-device, console and aux ports protected. Each one prevents a complete-device compromise or an unrecoverable situation, and together they fit in a week per site. P1, do it this quarter: CoPP baseline, routing protocol authentication, uRPF where the topology allows, DHCP snooping and dynamic ARP inspection on access, port security and BPDU guard, storm control, logging to a central collector. These reduce blast radius and stop the common access-layer attacks. P2, do it when the design settles: role-based command authorization, MACsec on select links, control plane protection tuning, per-class QoS verification, and any control whose value depends on another control already being in place. A footer lists what not to do at all: a second local account "for emergencies" that is never rotated, a shared admin password across a hundred devices, and a management VLAN that reaches every device from the user subnet.
svg.text: Hardening is a queue, not a checklist
P0 prevents total loss and fits in a week. Everything else can wait its turn without changing the risk much.
P0 THIS WEEK
Stops total device compromise
1 no management address reachable from the internet
2 SSH only, telnet and HTTP disabled
3 unique local credential plus central TACACS
4 SNMPv3 authPriv, or no SNMP at all
5 out-of-band access or a management VRF
6 NTP working and monitored
7 config backup automatic, stored off-device
8 console and aux ports physically protected
Each item alone can end in "the device is
no longer yours" - that is the test for P0.
effort: about a week per site, mostly scripting
and a maintenance window, not procurement
P1 THIS QUARTER
Reduces blast radius and stops the common attacks
CoPP baseline with per-class rates
routing protocol authentication, key rotation plan
uRPF where the topology is clean enough
DHCP snooping plus dynamic ARP inspection
port security, BPDU guard, root guard
storm control on access ports
logging to a collector that is not the device
802.1X where the endpoints permit it
These change how far an attacker gets once
inside - the risk reduction is large but the
failure mode is "one segment" not "all of it".
effort: a quarter, and it needs a test lab
P2 WHEN THE DESIGN SETTLES
Value depends on P1 existing
role-based command authorization
MACsec on selected links
CPPr fine tuning per sub-interface
per-class QoS verification
telemetry and anomaly baselines
control plane protection for IPv6 too
Doing these first is not harmful, it is
simply wasted: MACsec on a port whose
device password is "cisco" protects
the wrong thing.
Do not do these at all:
a shared admin password across a hundred devices, a second local account "for emergencies" that is never rotated, a management VLAN that is reachable from the user subnet.
The queue matters because security teams are always short of time: doing P2 while P0 is open is the most common way to spend a year and stay exposed.
Measure P0 completion as a percentage per site, published monthly. It is the one hardening metric that a manager can act on.
